canonical_statement: The study describes containment of a six-month, multi-unit hospital Candidozyma auris outbreak while testing evolved from culture to low- and high-throughput PCR alongside enhanced infection-prevention measures.
The outbreak occurred at Harborview Medical Center, a 500-bed urban public hospital in King County, Washington.
C. auris colonization was defined as a positive culture or PCR from skin, nares, respiratory tract, or urinary tract without signs of clinical C. auris infection.
Initial screening used composite axilla/groin and nares swabs with chromogenic culture followed by MALDI-TOF confirmation.

Low-throughput PCR used an ITS2-targeting laboratory-developed test on the BD MAX open channel, while high-throughput PCR used an ITS2-targeting laboratory-developed test on the cobas 8800 open channel.
Whole-genome sequencing was performed on available outbreak C. auris culture isolates and four isolates collected before the outbreak.
The Contact Plus precaution required standard personal protective equipment and EPA-registered disinfectants, including bleach or List P solutions for electronics.
Enhanced post-discharge decontamination included two terminal cleans, two UV-C treatments, and ATP monitoring with a target below 50 relative light units.
C. auris laboratory and testing-operations data were extracted from the laboratory information system and analyzed using R version 4.5.1.
The University of Washington Institutional Review Board approved the study with a waiver of informed consent (STUDY00000408).
Contact tracing after the first hospital-onset colonization event identified approximately 140 prior Unit A contacts; 48 still-admitted contacts were screened and one tested positive.

concept.text: Exposure to Unit A during outbreak investigation

canonical_statement: The state public health laboratory performed 100 screening tests during the initial phase with zero positive results and an average turnaround time of approximately 2 days from specimen receipt.

population.label: Specimens tested at state public health laboratory

canonical_statement: Culture-based screening performed 1,181 tests at an average of 18 tests per day and a median collection-to-result turnaround time of 82.1 hours (IQR 65.3-179.3).
Culture-based screening identified four positive cultures from three unique patients.
Low-throughput PCR enabled 1,539 tests at an average of 33 tests per day and reduced median collection-to-result turnaround time to 37.6 hours (IQR 35.6-39.8).

population.label: Low-throughput PCR C. auris screening tests

canonical_statement: Between outbreak weeks 3 and 7, twelve additional colonized patients were identified using low-throughput PCR and outside-facility test results.
House-wide screening was introduced because intensive contact tracing alone was difficult to sustain; by week 10 a high-throughput cobas 8800 PCR laboratory-developed test was validated.

The high-throughput PCR assay demonstrated a reported analytical limit of detection below 30 CFU/mL; detailed validation data were provided in Supplementary Tables S1-S3, which were not present in the packet PDF.
After high-throughput PCR validation, admission screening and weekly post-admission surveillance were implemented for all hospitalized patients through standard electronic admission order sets.
House-wide testing identified 16 additional C. auris-colonized patients over the subsequent three months.
Patients 11, 12, 17, and 20 had positive tests after occupying rooms previously used by known colonized patients despite routine terminal cleaning and UV-C treatment.
Following implementation of enhanced decontamination, no further transmission events from known colonized patients were observed.

Patients with hospital-acquired C. auris had an average of 2.72 inpatient bed moves before first positivity versus 1.17 moves in a random sample of 30 contemporaneous patients (Mann-Whitney U p=0.007).

population.label: Hospital-acquired C. auris patients and random contemporaneous controls

concept.text: Inpatient bed moves before first positive test

canonical_statement: Half of secondary transmission events were attributed to admission into rooms previously occupied by colonized individuals.

concept.text: Admission to a room previously occupied by a colonized patient

canonical_statement: From outbreak day 67 through day 163, 8,918 high-throughput PCR assays were performed at an average of 91 tests per day, and median collection-to-result turnaround time was 20.3 hours (IQR 12.4-30.5).
During the high-throughput period, 18 positive results represented 13 newly identified colonized individuals.
Across the six-month outbreak, 5,563 unique patients underwent C. auris testing, with a mean of 2.1 tests per person and 2,299 patients tested more than once.

population.label: Unique patients tested during the outbreak

concept.text: C. auris outbreak screening and surveillance

canonical_statement: The outbreak identified 29 C. auris-colonized patients and no associated clinical C. auris infections.

population.label: C. auris-colonized patients identified during outbreak

canonical_statement: Table 1 reports 5,537 patients with negative testing and 26 with positive testing in-system, with three outside-facility-only positives excluded from the table.
Whole-genome sequencing of five outbreak isolates showed all belonged to Clade I and formed a highly clonal cluster with pairwise SNP distances of 4 to 9 SNPs.
The pre-outbreak Clade I isolate was separated from the outbreak cluster by approximately 200 SNPs.

population.label: Pre-outbreak Clade I isolate and outbreak cluster

canonical_statement: All isolates with antifungal susceptibility testing were fluconazole resistant at greater than 64 micrograms/mL.

population.label: C. auris isolates with antifungal susceptibility testing

canonical_statement: Internal cost accounting estimated $310,000 in screening and surveillance reagents and $351,000 total when labor was included.

population.label: C. auris outbreak screening and surveillance program

canonical_statement: The reliance on PCR screening reduced the number of cultured isolates available for sequencing, so genomic data were insufficient to definitively map every transmission event.
Many PCR-only positive results had unknown viability, and without environmental cultures the study could not exclude residual environmental DNA from prior room occupants.
The amount of screening required for control may differ across hospitals because this facility had multiple congregate settings and substantial patient movement.
Because multiple interventions were introduced concurrently, the independent contribution of each intervention could not be determined.
The authors conclude that high-throughput PCR screening can help contain C. auris outbreaks when paired with rapid turnaround and rigorous infection-prevention practices.
The work received no specific funding.
Alexander L. Greninger reported multiple outside contract-testing, research-support, and personal-fee relationships; other conflict details were reported in the article disclosure section.
The article states that underlying data are available in the article and online supplementary material, with sequencing data deposited in NCBI SRA BioProject PRJNA1446860.

Figure 2 maps individual patients across time and bed spaces, distinguishing hospital-acquired detections, admission-screening positives, and negative surveillance tests.
